name: talking_head_ads
summary: What 12 editing-craft references agree on, cut down to what a single vertical talking-head clip can do (captions, headline, callouts, punch-in zooms, pace, end screen). Left out because the renderer cannot do them yet: B-roll, split screens, timeline/screen footage, picture-in-picture, sound effects, music, J/L cuts.

captions.notes: All 12 avoid word-by-word karaoke running over the whole video: use calm phrase-level captions and save big impact text for the one line that matters.

headline.notes: Big stacked uppercase for punchy hooks; a small tag for a calmer, informative tone.

callouts.notes: Labels and arrows tied to the exact words spoken; pill labels were the most common.

transitions.notes: Hard cuts and punch-in zooms only; every reference rejects whip pans, glitches, 3D spins and wipes.

end_screen.tone: A short, human closing line in the video's own voice (direct, playful or soft sell) with an understated button, not a big sales card.

rules: Change something on screen every 3 to 5 seconds (a punch-in, a callout, a headline change); never leave the talking head static longer than 5 seconds.
Punch in on punchlines, thesis statements and comedic or emotional beats; alternate wide and tight framing. Use them sparingly for serious topics.
Match pace to mood: trim dead air hard for energetic or comedic talk; keep natural pauses on serious or emotional lines so they can breathe.
Emphasise key words, numbers and punchlines with big bold uppercase centred text or a high-contrast pill label, not karaoke on every word.
Keep captions readable and calm: short phrases, clean shadow or pill style; save loud impact text for the one line that matters.
Callouts are labels and arrows tied to the exact words spoken: pop in for 2 to 4 seconds, two to five per ad, one at a time.
Use the headline to state the topic or hook: big stacked uppercase for a punchy hook, a small tag for a calmer, informative tone.
Keep the speaker's face clear: callouts sit to the side and never cover the face.
End on a short human closing line in the video's own voice with a small button or line, not a generic sales card.
Cut on complete sentences or thoughts; open with the strongest line or a question that the ending answers.
Contrast a burst of fast cutting with one held, quiet moment; a deliberate pause before a key line makes it land.
Vary the look and rhythm between ads in the same set instead of repeating one formula.
avoid: Word-by-word karaoke captions running over the whole video (every reference avoids them).
Static talking-head framing longer than 4 to 6 seconds with no punch-in, cut or overlay.
Flashy transitions: whip pans, glitches, 3D spins, page turns, light leaks, cheesy wipes, unmotivated dissolves.
Cluttered frames: stacked stickers, emojis or several overlays at once; give each moment one focal point.
Covering the speaker's face with graphics.
Punch-ins on every sentence or constant hyperactive zooming, especially on serious topics.
Over-trimming breath gaps on emotional lines, or frantic cutting with no room to breathe.
A generic or off-topic call to action, or sterile corporate lower-thirds.
